description:
Mars is far, the rockets pricey, the Moon is cold, the landings dicey.
So test it here, where Earth pretends: the dunes, the caves, the frozen ends.
We found the spots, we ranked the lot, Moon or Mars? Just book a slot.
summary:
Astronauts train for the Moon and Mars at analog sites on Earth, yet choosing those locations still relies on flat maps and guesswork. Eidolon fixes this. Powered by a custom ML search engine across 500,000+ Earth windows, it finds the closest 200 m terrain matches for any lunar or Martian target in seconds.

Crews can interactively inspect off-world targets beside their Earth doubles in 3D with elevation overlays and hill shades. Crucially, Eidolon separates pure terrain fidelity from practical suitability by taking into consideration climate, weather, and site access (including geopolitical stability, sovereign restrictions, infrastructure and distance from civilization). Using NASA POWER climatology, weather forecasts and solar shadow modeling, Eidolon pinpoints the best time to train at a site and then helps you book the campaign. Built on open NASA datasets (LRO LOLA, MGS MOLA, global DEMs), it works as a standalone app today and is designed to become part of NASA’s mission planning pipeline in the future.
details:
Exploring the Moon or Mars starts on Earth. Crews train at analog sites, places that look and behave like the world they’re heading to, but choosing those sites still relies on flat maps and word of mouth. Eidolon fixes this. Pick any place on the Moon or Mars and it finds the closest terrain on Earth, then helps you plan a test campaign there.

How It Works

  1. Pick a target. Choose from over 10,000 named IAU features, the candidate lunar south pole base regions (Malapert, Haworth, Nobile, de Gerlache), or drop a pin on any coordinate on the Moon or Mars.
  2. Fingerprint the terrain. Eidolon reads an 18.8 km elevation window around the target at 200 m resolution and turns it into a terrain fingerprint: landform shape and size, relief, slope, roughness, and whether the ground is raised or incised.
  3. Search the whole Earth. That fingerprint is matched against 500,127 Earth sites by a custom built ML search engine. Its a self-supervised neural network, trained by our team on elevation data, describes the terrain. A second model, the judge, then re-ranks the best matches the way a geologist would sort a shortlist. Named targets answer in milliseconds and custom coordinates in a few seconds.

Here's an example of a real result:

Search Nirgal Vallis on Mars for a rover mobility mission and the top match is on Hawaii’s Big Island, with a terrain score of 0.88. Shape, relief, slope and roughness all match. Landform size does not and Eidolon tells you so. It also tells you the site gets around 2,000 mm of rain a year, so the terrain is right but the climate is wrong.

What You Can Do With It

Crews can inspect the off-world target beside its Earth double in 3D, built from real elevation data, with terrain overlays, hill shades, slope maps, contour maps and measuring tools. Results can be filtered by country, sovereign access, and barren versus all land.

Eidolon scores terrain fidelity and practical suitability separately. Every site gets a grade from S to F after the user has chosen one out of the seven mission types - namely rover mobility, drilling and ISRU, EVA training, habitat operations, astrobiology and thermal testing. The grading takes into consideration climate, weather, operations and site access weighting each factor differently depending on the purpose of what needs to be trained.

This lets planners see the trade-off for themselves: the highest fidelity terrain might be in Antarctica, while the most workable match is a day’s drive away.

Some missions need more than open ground. When an established facility based analog such as HERA, CHAPEA or NEEMO’s undersea habitat covers more of a mission than any field site could, Eidolon lists it first. If a mission depends on gravity or radiation, it tells you to pair the site with a facility.

Once a site is chosen, NASA POWER climatology picks the best months to train, a 16-day weather forecast picks the best days, and a built-in booking flow lays out the campaign.

Target Science Context

We wanted crews to understand the place they’re training for as well as the place they’re training at. For every target, Eidolon shows what NASA has actually measured there. On the Moon: surface temperatures and rock abundance from LRO Diviner, plus lunar pits from the LROC atlas. On Mars: thermal inertia from THEMIS, water and rock chemistry from Mars Odyssey’s gamma-ray spectrometer, and nearby candidate cave entrances. On both: real NASA surface photographs, from Apollo to Perseverance.

Benefits & Impact

Analog campaigns cost money and crew hours, and a badly chosen site is a wasted training cycle. As NASA and its partners push towards a permanent base at the lunar south pole and crewed missions to Mars, that cost grows. Eidolon turns a slow, expert-only survey into a few minutes of exploration that anyone on a mission team can run and defend. Every result comes with the numbers behind it, so a site choice can be explained to the people paying for the campaign.

How We Built It

  • Moon data: LRO LOLA and LROC, plus the SLDEM2015 elevation merge with JAXA’s Kaguya.
  • Mars data: MGS MOLA blended with ESA’s HRSC, Viking colour mosaics and THEMIS.
  • Earth data: Copernicus elevation models, NASA POWER climatology, and NASA’s Blue Marble, Black Marble and MODIS imagery.
  • Frontend: TypeScript and three.js, built with Vite and no UI framework.
  • Engine: Python with PyTorch, GDAL and FastAPI.
  • Reliability: the two sides talk through a strict JSON Schema contract checked by automated tests, and everything runs on an ordinary laptop.
  • AI use: we used Claude Code as an AI coding assistant throughout, with full details in our README.

What Makes It Creative

Most analog work starts from a catalogue of sites people already know. Eidolon starts from the target and searches all of Earth’s land, so it can turn up places nobody has trained at before.

It also matches shadows. A sunlight simulation runs over both terrains and compares how much ground a low sun leaves in shadow. Shadows hide hazards from a rover’s cameras and a crew’s eyes, and we haven’t seen any other analog tool compare them.

And it doesn’t stop at finding a site. A built in booking flow turns a match into a campaign plan: you pick dates on a 14-day weather window that flags every day outside your mission’s weather limits, then add your team size and equipment. It gives an indicative cost based on how remote the site is, so a terrain search ends in a plan you can act on.

What We Considered

  • Accuracy. We tested the engine blind on 160 targets it had never seen. A good analog came first 34% of the time, in the top three 52.5% of the time, and in the top five 64% of the time. Where the engine is weak, such as lunar craters, every result says so.
  • Judgment. The mission weights are our team’s judgment. They are labelled as such in the app and backed by sources for which factors matter to which mission.
  • Licences and credit. Every dataset was vetted against the Space Apps licence terms, anything without a clear open licence was left out, and every image and map carries its attribution.
  • Accessibility. It works on mobile, passes WCAG accessibility checks, falls back to saved results if the engine is unreachable, and shows a poster version on devices without 3D graphics.

We want Eidolon to become part of NASA’s mission planning pipeline. Going forward, it will be shaped by the people using it: deeper planning for specific mission types, new engine features such as caves, and full integration with the way NASA processes and maps its own data.
